**W** ([minuscule](/wiki/Letter_case "Letter case"): **w**) is the twenty-third [letter](/wiki/Letter_(alphabet) "Letter (alphabet)") of the [Latin alphabet](/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), used in the [modern English alphabet](/wiki/English_alphabet "English alphabet"), the alphabets of other western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is [*double-u*](/wiki/English_alphabet#Letter_names "English alphabet"),[[in 1]](#cite_note-1) plural *double-ues*.[[1]](#cite_note-2)[[2]](#cite_note-3)

## Name

The name "double-u" reflects stages in the letter's evolution when it was considered two of the same letter, a double U.

Some speakers shorten the name "double u" into "dub-u" (in [Southern American accents](/wiki/Southern_American_English "Southern American English") this may be rendered as "[dubya](/wiki/Dubya "Dubya")"[[3]](#cite_note-The_Bush_Tragedy-4)) or simply as "dub"; for example, [University of Wisconsin](/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin "University of Wisconsin"), [University of Washington](/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington"), [University of Wyoming](/wiki/University_of_Wyoming "University of Wyoming"), [University of Waterloo](/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo"), [University of the Western Cape](/wiki/University_of_the_Western_Cape "University of the Western Cape") and [University of Western Australia](/wiki/University_of_Western_Australia "University of Western Australia") are all known colloquially as "U Dub", and the automobile company [Volkswagen](/wiki/Volkswagen "Volkswagen"), abbreviated "VW", is sometimes pronounced "V-Dub".[[4]](#cite_note-5)

In other [West Germanic languages](/wiki/West_Germanic_languages "West Germanic languages"), its name is monosyllabic: German *We* /veː/ (vs. *Vau* /fa͜ʊ/ for *v*), Dutch *wee* /ʋeː/ (vs. *vee* /veː/ for *v*). In [Polish](/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language") it is called *wu* /vu/ (vs. *fał* /faw/ or *we* /vɛ/ for *v*). In many languages, its name literally means "double v": Portuguese *duplo vê*,[[in 2]](#cite_note-6) Spanish *doble ve* (though it can be spelled *uve doble*),[[5]](#cite_note-7)[[in 3]](#cite_note-8) French *double vé*, [Icelandic](/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language") *tvöfalt vaff*, [Czech](/wiki/Czech_language "Czech language") *dvojité vé*, [Estonian](/wiki/Estonian_language "Estonian language") *kaksisvee*, [Finnish](/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language") *kaksois-vee*, etc.

The [classical Latin alphabet](/wiki/Latin_alphabet#Classical_Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), from which the modern European alphabets derived, did not have the "W" character. The "W" sounds were represented by the Latin letter "[V](/wiki/V "V")" (at the time, not yet distinct from "[U](/wiki/U "U")").

The sounds /[w](/wiki/Voiced_labial%E2%80%93velar_approximant "Voiced labial–velar approximant")/ (spelled ⟨V⟩) and /[b](/wiki/Voiced_bilabial_plosive "Voiced bilabial plosive")/ (spelled ⟨B⟩) of [Classical Latin](/wiki/Classical_Latin "Classical Latin") developed into the [voiced bilabial fricative](/wiki/Voiced_bilabial_fricative "Voiced bilabial fricative") /β/ between [vowels](/wiki/Vowel "Vowel") in [Early Medieval Latin](/wiki/Vulgar_Latin "Vulgar Latin"). Therefore, ⟨V⟩ no longer adequately represented the [voiced labial-velar approximant](/wiki/Voiced_labial-velar_approximant "Voiced labial-velar approximant") [sound](/wiki/Sound "Sound") /w/ of [Germanic phonology](/wiki/Common_Germanic "Common Germanic").

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Coat_of_arms_of_Vyborg.svg/250px-Coat_of_arms_of_Vyborg.svg.png)

The [Germanic](/wiki/German_language "German language") /w/ phoneme was therefore written as ⟨VV⟩ or ⟨uu⟩ by the earliest writers of [Old English](/wiki/Old_English "Old English") and [Old High German](/wiki/Old_High_German "Old High German") in the 7th or 8th centuries; ⟨[u](/wiki/U "U")⟩ and ⟨[v](/wiki/V "V")⟩ became distinct only by the [Early Modern period](/wiki/Early_Modern_period "Early Modern period").[[9]](#cite_note-12) [Gothic](/wiki/Gothic_alphabet "Gothic alphabet") (not [Latin-based](/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet")), by contrast, had simply used a letter based on the Greek [Υ](/wiki/Upsilon "Upsilon") for the same sound in the 4th century. The digraph ⟨VV⟩/⟨uu⟩ was also used in [Medieval Latin](/wiki/Medieval_Latin "Medieval Latin") to represent Germanic names, including Gothic ones like [Wamba](/wiki/Wamba,_Visigothic_king "Wamba, Visigothic king").

It is from this ⟨uu⟩ [digraph](/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") that the modern name "double U" derives. The digraph was commonly used in the spelling of Old High German but only in the earliest texts in Old English, where the /w/ sound soon came to be represented by borrowing the [rune](/wiki/Rune "Rune") ⟨ᚹ⟩, adapted as the Latin letter [wynn](/wiki/Wynn "Wynn"): ⟨ƿ⟩. In early [Middle English](/wiki/Middle_English "Middle English"), following the 11th-century [Norman Conquest](/wiki/Norman_Conquest_of_England "Norman Conquest of England"), ⟨uu⟩ regained popularity; by 1300, it had taken wynn's place in common use.

Scribal realisation of the digraph could look like a pair of Vs whose branches crossed in the middle: both forms (separate and crossed) appear, for instance, in the "running text" (in Latin) of the [Bayeux tapestry](/wiki/Bayeux_tapestry "Bayeux tapestry") in proper names such as EDVVARDVS and VVILLELMVS (or the same with crossed Vs). Another realisation (common in [italic](/wiki/Italic_type "Italic type"), [roundhand](/wiki/Roundhand "Roundhand"), [kurrent](/wiki/Kurrent "Kurrent"), [blackletter](/wiki/Blackletter "Blackletter"), and other scripts) takes a form like an ⟨n⟩ whose rightmost branch curved around, as in a ⟨v⟩ (viz.

It was probably considered a separate letter by the 14th century in both [Middle English](/wiki/Middle_English "Middle English") and [Middle German](/wiki/Middle_Low_German "Middle Low German") orthography. However, it remained an outsider, not really considered part of the Latin alphabet proper, as expressed by [Valentin Ickelshamer](/wiki/Valentin_Ickelshamer "Valentin Ickelshamer") in the 16th century, who complained that:

Poor *w* is so infamous and unknown that many barely know either its name or its shape, not those who aspire to being Latinists, as they have no need of it, nor do the Germans, not even the schoolmasters, know what to do with it or how to call it; some call it *we*, [... others] call it *uu*, [...] the [Swabians](/wiki/Swabians "Swabians") call it *auwawau*[[10]](#cite_note-14)

In [Middle High German](/wiki/Middle_High_German "Middle High German") (and possibly already in late Old High German), the West Germanic phoneme /w/ became realized as [[v](/wiki/Voiced_labiodental_fricative "Voiced labiodental fricative")]; this is why, today, the German ⟨w⟩ represents that sound.

### English

English uses ⟨w⟩ to represent /w/. There are also a number of words beginning with a written ⟨w⟩ that are [silent](/wiki/Silent_letter "Silent letter") in most dialects before a (pronounced) ⟨r⟩, remaining from usage in [Old English](/wiki/Old_English_language "Old English language") in which the ⟨w⟩ was pronounced: *wreak*, *wrap*, *wreck*, *wrench*, *wroth*, *wrinkle*, etc. Certain dialects of [Scottish English](/wiki/Scottish_English "Scottish English") still distinguish this digraph. ⟨w⟩ represents a vowel sound, /oʊ/, in the word [pwn](/wiki/Pwn "Pwn"), and in the Welsh loanwords [*cwm*](/wiki/Cwm_(landform) "Cwm (landform)") and *[crwth](/wiki/Crwth "Crwth")*, it retains the Welsh pronunciation, /ʊ/. ⟨w⟩ is also used in digraphs: ⟨aw⟩ /ɔː/, ⟨ew⟩ /(j)uː/, ⟨ow⟩ /aʊ, oʊ/, wherein it is usually an orthographic [allograph](/wiki/Allograph "Allograph") of ⟨u⟩ in final positions. It is the [fifteenth most frequently used letter](/wiki/Letter_frequency "Letter frequency") in the English language, with a frequency of about 2.56% in words.

### Other languages

In Europe languages with ⟨w⟩ in native words are in a central-western European zone between Cornwall and Poland: English, [German](/wiki/German_language "German language"), [Low German](/wiki/Low_German_language "Low German language"), [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"), [Frisian](/wiki/Frisian_languages "Frisian languages"), [Welsh](/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language"), [Cornish](/wiki/Cornish_language "Cornish language"), [Breton](/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"), [Walloon](/wiki/Walloon_language "Walloon language"), [Polish](/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"), [Kashubian](/wiki/Kashubian_language "Kashubian language"), [Sorbian](/wiki/Sorbian_languages "Sorbian languages"), [Wymysorys](/wiki/Wymysorys_language "Wymysorys language"), [Resian](/wiki/Resian_dialect "Resian dialect") and [Scandinavian dialects](/wiki/North_Germanic_languages "North Germanic languages"). German, Polish, Wymysorys and Kashubian use it for the [voiced labiodental fricative](/wiki/Voiced_labiodental_fricative "Voiced labiodental fricative") /v/ (with Polish, related Kashubian and Wymysorys using [Ł](/wiki/%C5%81 "Ł") for /w/, except in conservative and some eastern Polish speech, where Ł still represents the [dark L](/wiki/Dark_L "Dark L") sound.), and Dutch uses it for /ʋ/. Unlike its use in other languages, the letter is used in [Welsh](/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language") and [Cornish](/wiki/Cornish_language "Cornish language") to represent the vowel /u/ as well as the related approximant consonant /w/.

It is also used in modern systems of [Romanization of Belarusian](/wiki/Romanization_of_Belarusian "Romanization of Belarusian") for the letter ⟨[ў](/wiki/%D0%8E "Ў")⟩, for example in the BGN/PCGN[[11]](#cite_note-:0-15) system, in contrast to the letter ⟨[ŭ](/wiki/%C5%AC "Ŭ")⟩, which is used in the [Instruction on transliteration of Belarusian geographical names with letters of Latin script](/wiki/Instruction_on_transliteration_of_Belarusian_geographical_names_with_letters_of_Latin_script "Instruction on transliteration of Belarusian geographical names with letters of Latin script").

In Swedish and Finnish, traces of this old usage may still be found in proper names. In [Hungarian](/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language") remains in some aristocratic surnames, e.g. [Wesselényi](/wiki/Wessel%C3%A9nyi_(disambiguation) "Wesselényi (disambiguation)").

Modern [German dialects](/wiki/German_dialects "German dialects") generally have only [v] or [ʋ] for West Germanic /w/, but [w] or [β̞] is still heard allophonically for ⟨w⟩, especially in the clusters ⟨schw⟩, ⟨zw⟩, and ⟨qu⟩. Some Bavarian dialects preserve a "light" initial [w], such as in *wuoz* (Standard German *weiß* [vaɪs] '[I] know'). The Classical Latin [β] is heard in the Southern German greeting *Servus* ('hello' or 'goodbye').

In [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"), ⟨w⟩ became a [labiodental approximant](/wiki/Labiodental_approximant "Labiodental approximant") /ʋ/ (with the exception of words with -⟨eeuw⟩, which have /eːβ/, or other diphthongs containing -⟨uw⟩). In many Dutch-speaking areas, such as [Flanders](/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and [Suriname](/wiki/Suriname "Suriname"), the /β/ pronunciation (or in some areas a /ɥ/ pronunciation, e.g. Belgian-Dutch *water* /'ɥaːtər/ "water", *wit* /ɥɪt/ "white", *eeuw* /eːɥ/ "century", etc.) is used at all times.

In [Finnish](/wiki/Finnish_alphabet "Finnish alphabet"), ⟨w⟩ is sometimes seen as a variant of ⟨v⟩ and not a separate letter, but it is a part of the official alphabet. It is, however, recognized and maintained in the spelling of some old names, reflecting an earlier German spelling standard, and in some modern loan words. In all cases, it is pronounced /ʋ/. The title of the first edition of the *[Kalevala](/wiki/Kalevala "Kalevala")* was spelled *Kalewala*.

In [Danish](/wiki/Danish_alphabet "Danish alphabet"), [Norwegian](/wiki/Norwegian_alphabet "Norwegian alphabet") and [Swedish](/wiki/Swedish_alphabet "Swedish alphabet"), ⟨w⟩ is named double-v and not double-u. In these languages, the letter only exists in old names, loanwords and foreign words. (Foreign words are distinguished from loanwords by having a significantly lower level of integration in the language.) It is usually pronounced /v/, but in some words of English origin, it may be pronounced /w/.[[12]](#cite_note-16)[[13]](#cite_note-17) The letter was officially introduced in the Danish and Swedish alphabets as late as 1980 and 2006, respectively, despite having been in use for much longer. It had been recognized since the conception of modern Norwegian with the earliest official orthography rules of 1907.[[14]](#cite_note-18) ⟨W⟩ was earlier seen as a variant of ⟨v⟩, and ⟨w⟩ as a letter (double-v) is still commonly replaced by ⟨v⟩ in speech (e.g. *WC* being pronounced as *VC*, *www* as *VVV*, *WHO* as *VHO*, etc.). The two letters were sorted as equals before ⟨w⟩ was officially recognized, and that practice is still recommended when sorting names in Sweden.[[15]](#cite_note-19) In modern slang, some native speakers may pronounce ⟨w⟩ more closely to the origin of the loanword than the official /v/ pronunciation.

Multiple dialects of Swedish and Danish use the sound, however. In Denmark, notably in [Jutland](/wiki/Jutland "Jutland"), the northern half uses it extensively in [traditional dialect](/wiki/Jutlandic_dialect "Jutlandic dialect"), and in multiple places in Sweden. It is used in southern Swedish; for example, the words "wesp" (wisp) and "wann" (water) are traditionally used in [Halland](/wiki/Halland "Halland").[[16]](#cite_note-20) In northern and western Sweden, there are also dialects with /w/. [Elfdalian](/wiki/Elfdalian "Elfdalian") is a good example, which is one of many dialects where the [Old Norse difference](/wiki/Old_Norse_orthography "Old Norse orthography") between v (/w/) and f (/v/ or /f/) is preserved. Thus, "warg" from Old Norse "vargr", but "åvå" from Old Norse "hafa".

In the alphabets of most modern Romance languages, ⟨w⟩ is used mostly in foreign names and words recently borrowed (Italian *il watt*, Spanish *el kiwi*). In Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese, [w] is a non-syllabic variant of /u/, spelled ⟨u⟩. In French, ⟨w⟩ is also used mostly in foreign names and words recently borrowed such as *wagon* or *week*(*-*)*end*, but in the first case it is pronounced [v] (because of its German origin; except in Belgium, where it is pronounced [w]) and in the second [w]. In most northern French dialects, the former ⟨w⟩ turned finally to ⟨v⟩, but still exists as a remnant in the place-names of [Romance Flanders](/wiki/Romance_Flanders "Romance Flanders"), [Picardie](/wiki/Picardie "Picardie"), [Artois](/wiki/Artois "Artois"), [Champagne](/wiki/Champagne "Champagne"), [Romance Lorraine](/wiki/Lorraine "Lorraine") and sometimes elsewhere ([Normandy](/wiki/Normandy "Normandy"), [Île-de-France](/wiki/%C3%8Ele-de-France "Île-de-France")), and in the surnames from the same regions. Walloon as it sounds conserves the ⟨w⟩ pronounced [w]. The digraph ⟨ou⟩ is used to render ⟨w⟩ in rare French words such as *ouest* "west" and to spell Arabic names transliterated *-wi* in English, but *-oui* in French (compare Arabic surname [Badawi](/wiki/Badawi "Badawi") / Badaoui). In all these languages, as in Scandinavian languages mentioned above, the letter is named "double v" (French /dubləve/, Spanish /'dɔble 'uβe/) though in Belgium the name /we/ is also used.

In [Indonesian](/wiki/Indonesian_language "Indonesian language"), the letter "w" is called *wé*. The letter names in Indonesian are always the same with the sounds they produce, especially the consonants.

The [Japanese language](/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language") uses "W", pronounced *daburu*, as an ideogram meaning "double".[[17]](#cite_note-21) It is also used in internet slang to indicate laughter (like [LOL](/wiki/LOL#Commonly_used_equivalents_in_other_languages "LOL")), derived from the word *warau* (笑う, meaning "to laugh").

In [Italian](/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"), while the letter ⟨w⟩ is not considered part of the standard [Italian alphabet](/wiki/Italian_alphabet "Italian alphabet"), the character is often used in place of *[Viva](/wiki/Vive,_viva,_and_vivat "Vive, viva, and vivat")* ("hooray for..."), generally in the form in which the branches of the Vs cross in the middle, at least in [handwriting](/wiki/Handwriting "Handwriting") (in fact, it could be considered a [monogram](/wiki/Monogram "Monogram")).[[18]](#cite_note-Zingarelli_1945_1713-22) The same symbol written upside down indicates *abbasso* ("down with...").

In the [Kokborok language](/wiki/Kokborok "Kokborok"), ⟨w⟩ represents the [open-mid back rounded vowel](/wiki/Open-mid_back_rounded_vowel "Open-mid back rounded vowel") /ɔ/.

In Turkey, the use of the ⟨w⟩ was banned between 1928 and 2013[[19]](#cite_note-:1-23)[[20]](#cite_note-24) which was a problem for the [Kurdish population in Turkey](/wiki/Kurds_in_Turkey "Kurds in Turkey") as the ⟨w⟩ was a letter of the [Kurdish alphabet](/wiki/Kurdish_alphabets "Kurdish alphabets").[[21]](#cite_note-25) The use of the letter ⟨w⟩ in the word [Newroz](/wiki/Newroz_as_celebrated_by_Kurds "Newroz as celebrated by Kurds"), the Kurdish new year, was forbidden,[[22]](#cite_note-:2-26) and names which included the letter were not able to be used.[[19]](#cite_note-:1-23)[[23]](#cite_note-27) In 2008, a court in [Gaziantep](/wiki/Gaziantep "Gaziantep") reasoned the use of the letter ⟨w⟩ would incite civil unrest.[[22]](#cite_note-:2-26)

In [Vietnamese](/wiki/Vietnamese_language "Vietnamese language"), ⟨w⟩ is called **vê đúp** or *vê kép* (lit. 'double V'), from the French **double vé**. It is not included in the standard [Vietnamese alphabet](/wiki/Vietnamese_alphabet "Vietnamese alphabet"), but it is often used as a substitute for *qu-* in [literary dialect](/wiki/Literary_dialect "Literary dialect") and very informal writing.[[24]](#cite_note-28)[[25]](#cite_note-29) It's also commonly used for abbreviating *Ư* in formal documents, for example *Trung Ương* is abbreviated as TW[[26]](#cite_note-30) even in official documents and document ID number, derived from the [Vietnamese Telex input method](/wiki/Telex_(input_method) "Telex (input method)") that usually interpret a single "w" into Vietnamese character "ư".[[27]](#cite_note-31)

"W" is the 24th letter in the [Modern Filipino Alphabet](/wiki/Filipino_alphabet "Filipino alphabet") and has its English name. However, in the old Filipino alphabet, [Abakada](/wiki/Abakada "Abakada"), it was the 19th letter and had the name "wah".[*[is that 'h' a glottal stop?](/wiki/Wikipedia:Cleanup "Wikipedia:Cleanup")*][[28]](#cite_note-32)

In [Washo](/wiki/Washo_language "Washo language"), lower-case ⟨w⟩ represents a typical /w/ sound, while upper-case ⟨W⟩ represents a [voiceless](/wiki/Voicelessness "Voicelessness") w sound, like the difference between English *weather* and *whether* for those who maintain the distinction.

***W*** is a monthly American fashion [magazine](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine "Magazine") published by Condé Nast Publications. It was started in 1972 by the publisher of sister magazine [Woman's Wear Daily](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman's_Wear_Daily?action=edit&redlink=1 "Woman's Wear Daily (not yet started)"), James Brady. The magazine is an oversize set – ten [inches](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inches "Inches") wide and thirteen inches tall. W magazine has nearly half a million, 469,000 subscribers. 80 percent of the magazine's readers are girls and women. [[2]](#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American fashion magazine

W [...] W (stylized in all caps), also known as W Magazine, is an American bi-monthly fashion magazine that covers fashion, culture, entertainment, beauty, life, and travel. Since 2019, Sara Moonves has overseen the magazine's editorial content as editor-in-chief. John Fairchild "John Fairchild (editor)"), from 1972 was the first editor, remaining in the position until 1997 when Patrick McCarthy "Patrick McCarthy (publisher)") took over the role, Stefano Tonchi served as editor-in-chief from 2010 until Moonves appointment in 2019.

***W*** (stylized in [all caps](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_caps "All caps")), also known as ***W Magazine***, is an American bi-monthly [fashion magazine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_magazine "Fashion magazine") that covers fashion, culture, entertainment, beauty, life, and travel. Since 2019, [Sara Moonves](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Moonves "Sara Moonves") has overseen the magazine's editorial content as editor-in-chief. [John Fairchild](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fairchild_(editor) "John Fairchild (editor)"), from 1972 was the first editor, remaining in the position until 1997 when [Patrick McCarthy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_McCarthy_(publisher) "Patrick McCarthy (publisher)") took over the role, [Stefano Tonchi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Tonchi "Stefano Tonchi") served as editor-in-chief from 2010 until Moonves appointment in 2019.

Based at [One World Trade Center](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center "One World Trade Center") in the [Financial District](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FiDi "FiDi") of [New York City](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") it began publication in 1972 as a bi-weekly supplement to the fashion trade newspaper, *[Women's Wear Daily](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Wear_Daily "Women's Wear Daily")*.[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 1993, the publication transitioned into a monthly magazine and was no longer a supplement to *Women's Wear Daily*.

*[W Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W_Korea "W Korea")* launched in 2005 and is the oldest continuously operating international edition of *W*, *[W China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W_China "W China")* launched in 2023 and is distributed across Mainland China. In September 2026, a youth culture-focused spinoff titled *[W Youth](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W_Youth?action=edit&redlink=1 "W Youth (page does not exist)")* will launch.

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

*W* was launched in 1972.[[3]](#cite_note-Fashion_Theory-3) The magazine was published as a bi-weekly until 1993, when it was relaunched as an oversized publication published on a monthly schedule.

In 1999, [Condé Nast](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condé_Nast "Condé Nast") purchased the magazine from [Fairchild Publications](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Publications "Fairchild Publications"). In 2019, it was sold to *Surface Media* (later renamed *Future Media Group*) and in 2020 it was sold to *W Media* which was created for the purchase. It now operates in partnership with [Bustle Digital Group](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bustle_Digital_Group "Bustle Digital Group") and Mic, along with a group of investors (led by [Karlie Kloss](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlie_Kloss "Karlie Kloss")).

The magazine is currently published every other month, alongside a summer special issue (seven times per year).

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

### Origins of W, under Fairchild Fashion Media, 1972–1999

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Origins of W, under Fairchild Fashion Media, 1972–1999")]

W Magazine origins lie as a biweekly newspaper, which was spun off from *Women's Wear Daily*,[[8]](#cite_note-nytimes.com-9) becoming an oversized monthly magazine published by [Fairchild Fashion Media](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Fashion_Media "Fairchild Fashion Media") in 1993. When Fairchilds' owner ([Capital Cities/ABC](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Cities/ABC "Capital Cities/ABC")) merged with [The Walt Disney Company](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Company "Walt Disney Company") in 1997, *W* was one of the publications the new company continued to publish.[[9]](#cite_note-10)

### Under Condé Nast, 1999–2019

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Under Condé Nast, 1999–2019")]

*W* has garnered controversy over some of the featured models in its issues. Controversial cover shoots include [Steven Meisel](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Meisel "Steven Meisel")'s entitled "[Asexual](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asexuality "Asexuality") Revolution", in which male and female models (including [Jessica Stam](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Stam "Jessica Stam") and [Karen Elson](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Elson "Karen Elson")) are depicted in gender-bending styles and provocative poses. In addition, [Tom Ford](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Ford "Tom Ford")'s racy shoot with Klein and the accompanying article on sexuality in fashion came as a shock to some loyal readers. During the interview, Ford is quoted as saying: "I've always been about [pansexuality](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pansexuality "Pansexuality"). Whether I'm sleeping with girls or not at this point in my life, the clothes have often been [androgynous](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgynous "Androgynous"), which is very much my standard of [beauty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty "Beauty")".[[10]](#cite_note-Fordbitten-11) Klein was also the photographer for the racy photo shoot featured in the August 2007 issue, showcasing [David](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") and [Victoria Beckham](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Beckham "Victoria Beckham").[[11]](#cite_note-12) [Bruce Weber](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Weber_(photographer) "Bruce Weber (photographer)") produced a 60-page tribute to [New Orleans](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") in the April 2008 issue, and shot a 36-page story on the newest fashion designers in [Miami](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami") for the July 2008 issue.[[12]](#cite_note-Come_on_Down_to_Nawlins-13)[[13]](#cite_note-Summer_Camp-14)

In 2009 due to the [2008 Financial Crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), advertising pages in the magazine were down 46 percent from 2008.[[14]](#cite_note-15) Editor-in-Chief [Patrick McCarthy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_McCarthy_(publisher) "Patrick McCarthy (publisher)") retired in 2010 when Condé Nast moved *W* into its consumer magazine group, now alongside *[Vogue](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")*, *[Glamour](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamour_(magazine) "Glamour (magazine)")* and *[Allure](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allure_(magazine) "Allure (magazine)")*.[[8]](#cite_note-nytimes.com-9) [Stefano Tonchi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Tonchi "Stefano Tonchi") succeeded him as editor in chief.[[15]](#cite_note-16) [Edward Enninful](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Enninful "Edward Enninful") was appointed Fashion & Style Director in 2011.[[16]](#cite_note-17)[[17]](#cite_note-18) In 2011, *W* participated in a four-episode plot line on the [fourth season](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossip_Girl_(season_4) "Gossip Girl (season 4)") of [CW](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_CW "The CW") teen drama [Gossip Girl](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossip_Girl "Gossip Girl").[[18]](#cite_note-19)

Under Enninful's direction, *W* introduced riskier editorial features, including the March 2012 cover story by [Steven Klein](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Klein_(artist) "Steven Klein (artist)") that depicted [Kate Moss](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Moss "Kate Moss") as a nun and [Nicki Minaj](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicki_Minaj "Nicki Minaj") portraying an 18th-century French courtesan.[[19]](#cite_note-20)

Between 2013 and 2018 the magazine went from publishing twelve issues per year to eight.[[20]](#cite_note-21) This would later be reduced to four in 2020, raise to six from 2021, and W currently publishes seven issues a year 2024.

### Under Future Media, 2019–2020

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Under Future Media, 2019–2020")]

In 2018, *W* became one of three publications Condé Nast put up for sale in the face of significant financial losses that forced it to adopt a series of cost-cutting measures. By 2019, it was acquired by Future Media, in a deal the *[New York Post](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post "New York Post")* estimated at $7 million.[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-23) In June 2019, [Sara Moonves](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Moonves "Sara Moonves") was named as the publications first female editor-in-chief, succeeding [Stefano Tonchi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Tonchi "Stefano Tonchi").[[23]](#cite_note-Marc_Tracy_2019-24)

Under Moonves's editorship, the magazine underwent a major transition. By 2020, she announced to staff that many were being furloughed and that those who work on online content would be staying on at reduced salaries.[[24]](#cite_note-Jacob_Bernstein_2020-25) The new *W* team finished the biggest Best Performances issue ever. In the first week of January 2020, *W* launched nine covers, and a 76-page celebrity portfolio covering 29 celebrities and 20 videos.[[25]](#cite_note-Brad_Pitt-26) Additionally, the magazine launched a series of new initiatives and expanded its digital footprint. Launching *W*’s first [podcast](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast"), *5 Things with [Lynn Hirschberg](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Hirschberg "Lynn Hirschberg")*, which attracted included guests including [Quentin Tarantino](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino"), [Charlize Theron](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlize_Theron "Charlize Theron"), [Saoirse Ronan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saoirse_Ronan "Saoirse Ronan"), [Greta Gerwig](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Gerwig "Greta Gerwig"), [Noah Baumbach](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Baumbach "Noah Baumbach"), [Nicole Kidman](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Kidman "Nicole Kidman"), [Awkwafina](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awkwafina "Awkwafina"), and [Margot Robbie](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margot_Robbie "Margot Robbie") as a part of the new vision for the brand.[[26]](#cite_note-5_Things-27)

### Under *W Media*, 2020–present

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Under W Media, 2020–present")]

On August 14, 2020, *W* was acquired by [Bustle Digital Group](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bustle_(magazine) "Bustle (magazine)"), [Mic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mic_(media_company) "Mic (media company)"),[[22]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-23)[[27]](#cite_note-fashionweekdaily2020-08-14-28) and W Media, a newly formed joint venture led by [Karlie Kloss](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlie_Kloss "Karlie Kloss") and including [Aryeh Bourkoff](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryeh_Bourkoff "Aryeh Bourkoff"), [Jason Blum](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Blum "Jason Blum"), [Kaia Gerber](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaia_Gerber "Kaia Gerber"), [Kirsten Green](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsten_Green "Kirsten Green") and [Lewis Hamilton](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton").[[28]](#cite_note-29) Moonves was kept as editor-in-chief.

## International editions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=W_(magazine)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: International editions")]

International editions were previously published in Japan and for Europe. The European edition launched in 1991 as *W Fashion Life* and separate versions were released in English, French, and Italian. In 1992 the magazine rebranded to *W Fashion Europe*. *W Fashion Europe* ceased publication in 1994.

The [South Korean](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") edition was launched in 2005 and is published under license by [*Doosan Magazine*](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doosan_Group "Doosan Group").[[29]](#cite_note-Doosan_Group-30) A Chinese edition was launched in 2023 under license by MC Style Media; the magazine's editor-in-chief is Mix Wei.[[30]](#cite_note-:0-31)
